A group of Utah residents just decided they're done being ignored — and they're taking the fight to court.

The Alliance for a Better Utah and five Box Elder County residents filed suit Wednesday in Utah's 3rd District Court over the approval of Kevin O'Leary's "Stratos Project" — a sprawling AI data center planned for the rural Hansel Valley. Their core argument is simple but explosive: the people who actually live there were never given a real say.

The lawsuit targets the Military Installation Development Authority, or MIDA — an unelected body that signed off on the project. Plaintiffs say MIDA exercised powers "the Utah Constitution never authorized," approving a development that could reshape residents' water, land, environment, and daily lives without any democratic vote. It also names the Box Elder County Commission, Senate President J. Stuart Adams, and state Sen. Jerry Stevenson.

Here's the part raising eyebrows: Adams and Stevenson are sitting legislators who also serve on the MIDA board. The suit argues that holding both roles may violate Utah's ban on occupying more than one office of public trust at once — and that it should render the project's approval null and void.

The pressure is already working. O'Leary has conceded to shrinking the original 40,000-acre footprint by roughly 75%, committing water to the shrinking Great Salt Lake, and setting aside thousands of acres for open space, wildlife, and farming. But the plaintiffs want the court to throw out the approval entirely and permanently block the plan.

The question now: can a handful of residents stop a billionaire's data center empire — and force their own government to answer for how it got approved?

O'Leary is also responsible for the Wonder Valley Data Center by Grande Prairie, where they are in serious drought.

Stratos project investor Kevin O’Leary has agreed to conditions outlined in a June 1 demand letter from Utah Senate President Stuart Adams, including reducing the size of the proposed data center and dedicating new water to the Great Salt Lake, according to a statement issued by Adam’s office Thursday morning.

My financials are public record from my 2024 Senate run. I’ve never taken a dollar from BEAR or Earthly Education.

So NBC, host me. A rebuttal, or a live debate with Kevin. You gave him 16 minutes. Give Utah our time too. 

The one thing he’s actually accomplished is uniting us. Republicans, Democrats, independents, people who’ve never voted, standing up together against a genuine foreign threat.

A proposed 40,000-acre data center campus in northern Utah is drawing increasing attention from state leaders and local residents as concerns grow over its size, resource demands, and potential environmental impact.

The project, backed by investor Kevin O’Leary, would be built near the Great Salt Lake, a region already facing long-term environmental challenges. In response to public concerns, Utah Senate President Stuart Adams announced that he has formally requested a significant reduction in the project's footprint.

In a statement released Monday, Adams said he sent a letter to O’Leary calling for the proposed development area to be reduced by 75%, from 40,000 acres to approximately 10,000 acres. He also stated that any excess water associated with the project should be treated and dedicated to supporting the Great Salt Lake.

Adams, who serves on the board of the Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA) — the agency overseeing the project in Box Elder County — said additional safeguards are needed as the development moves through the review process.

The proposal has generated widespread public discussion in recent weeks, with critics raising concerns about water consumption, energy use, emissions, and the overall scale of the project. Supporters, meanwhile, point to the potential economic benefits and technological investment it could bring to the region.

Adams also called for greater transparency, stronger conservation measures, and enhanced protections for Utah’s natural resources.

“Utah can pursue economic opportunity while protecting our water, air, wildlife, and communities,” Adams said. “We can and must do both.”

The project remains under review as state officials, developers, and community members continue to debate its future and potential impact on the region.

More than 600 people packed the Utah State Capitol this week to push back against a proposed data center the size of a small city — and they say the Great Salt Lake could pay the price.

The project, known as "Wonder Valley" (also called Stratos), would span roughly 40,000 acres in Box Elder County. It's backed by "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary, who has pitched it as a major economic engine that could bring jobs, infrastructure, and billions in investment to northern Utah.

But the residents who rallied at the Capitol have one overriding concern: water. Data centers consume enormous amounts of it for cooling, and the Great Salt Lake has already been shrinking for years. Opponents fear a development this large could draw down the water supply even further and accelerate the lake's decline — a problem that affects air quality, wildlife, and the regional economy.

Supporters of the project argue it could be designed with water-efficient cooling and would deliver long-term economic benefits to a rural part of the state. Backers also point to growing demand for computing power and the chance for Utah to become a hub for it.

For now, the two sides are far apart. The crowd at the Capitol made clear that any project touching the Great Salt Lake's water will face serious public scrutiny before it moves forward.

Hundreds of Utahns descended on the state capitol on May 23rd with a blunt message: Kevin O'Leary's massive data center project is not welcome near the Great Salt Lake. The crowd chanted "data center dollars don't trickle down, Kevin O'Leary get out of our town" as speakers warned about what could happen to one of America's most fragile ecosystems if the project moves forward.

The project — called the Stratos Hyperscale Data Center — is a proposed 40,000-acre AI data center campus in Box Elder County, right along the northern shore of the Great Salt Lake. One data center. One of America’s driest states. 3,700 formal water protests. Mermaids at the state Capitol. A TV investor blaming China. A mother with her infant son standing in the heat saying “we can’t get this back.”

And Congress — doing absolutely nothing.

This is the story of Utah versus the Stratos Project. And it is the most dramatic, most emotional, most consequential data center battle happening anywhere in America right now.

Published June 11, 2026 by Roll Call. 100% real. 100% verified. And it is exploding across the internet today.

🏜️ WHAT IS THE STRATOS PROJECT — AND WHY IS IT UNLIKE ANYTHING AMERICA HAS SEEN BEFORE

The Stratos Project is a proposed AI data center development in Box Elder County, Utah — a rural, remote stretch of desert in the northwestern corner of one of America’s driest states.

At its original proposed scale — the project would have covered 40,000 acres. That is larger than Bryce Canyon National Park. Larger than the entire city of Washington D.C. One of the most famous natural landscapes in all of America — in a state that is already starving for water.

Residents from a state starving for water have become the face of local struggles against Big Tech, locked in protests against a proposed data center that at one point was set to sprawl thousands of acres larger than its infamous Bryce Canyon. ￼

40,000 acres of Utah desert. Earmarked for an AI data center campus. In a state with one of the most severe water crises in the entire country.

And nobody asked the people of Utah first.

💧 THE WATER NUMBERS THAT EXPLAIN EVERYTHING

Here is the detail that ignited this entire fight — and that makes every Utahn’s blood run cold.

The developers were originally seeking 13,000 acre-feet of rights to groundwater in Utah. ￼ One acre-foot of water equals 325,851 gallons. 13,000 acre-feet equals more than 4.2 BILLION gallons of groundwater — from one of the driest states in America.

And the electricity demand was even more staggering. While developers say Stratos wouldn’t rely on Utah’s existing electric grid — it was once proposed to use more than double the electricity currently consumed by the entire state. ￼

More than double the electricity consumption of the entire state of Utah. For one data center campus. In a desert.

The proposed mega data center needs to change a water right from agricultural to industrial use. Opponents want to prevent that from happening. ￼

Agricultural water — water that feeds Utah’s farms, its communities, its livestock — being redirected to cool AI servers. That is the trade Utah was being asked to make.

😤 THE MOMENT THAT MADE UTAH EXPLODE — A VOTE WITH NO PUBLIC COMMENT

The fury in Utah did not build slowly. It erupted the moment people found out what their government had done without them.

On April 24, the appointed, seven-member board of Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority, or MIDA, gave its approval for the proposal. Ten days later, Box Elder County commissioners voted to keep it moving forward during a tense meeting where protesters shouted in opposition. The commission did not take public comment before voting on May 4. ￼

Read that again. The commission did not take public comment. Before voting on one of the largest development proposals in Utah’s history. A project larger than Bryce Canyon. Using billions of gallons of groundwater. And the public was not allowed to speak.

“Utahns do not feel heard,” Jayden Weekes of Cache County said from a podium at the rally Thursday, balancing one of her young children on her hip. ￼

A mother. A baby on her hip. At a rally at the state Capitol. Because her government voted on a 40,000-acre project and did not let her speak.

🧜 THE IMAGE THAT WENT AROUND THE WORLD — MERMAIDS AT THE UTAH CAPITOL

The protest movement in Utah did not just show up with signs. It showed up with creativity — and with an image so striking it went viral nationwide.

Mermaids at the Utah Capitol protest the 40,000-acre Stratos data center in Box Elder County on May 14, 2026. ￼

Protesters dressed as mermaids. At the Utah State Capitol. Protesting a data center that wants to drain Utah’s groundwater.

The symbolism was perfect. Mermaids — creatures of the water — standing on the dry steps of a government building to say: if you drain our water for a data center, there will be nothing left for the creatures that depend on it.

The images went everywhere. And they brought national attention to a fight that had previously been contained to rural Box Elder County.

💪 MORE THAN 600 UTAHNS RALLIED — AND 3,700 FILED FORMAL WATER PROTESTS

The mermaids were just the beginning.

More than 600 people rallied at the Capitol on Saturday afternoon, calling for an end to the proposed data center development in Box Elder County. ￼

Christaline Cornell braved the heat Saturday with her infant son to stand on the steps of the state Capitol and protest the Stratos Project, saying his future is the reason she had to attend. “The water, the food, the planet, the environment — we can’t get that back once we take it away,” the American Fork woman said. ￼

A mother. Standing in the Utah heat. Holding her infant son. Fighting for his future.

And the formal legal resistance was just as powerful. More than 3,700 protests were lodged over water rights for the Box Elder data center. ￼

3,700 formal legal protests. Over water rights. Filed by Utah residents who refused to let their groundwater be taken without a fight.

🦈 KEVIN O’LEARY BLAMED CHINA. UTAH WASN’T BUYING IT

The man behind the Stratos Project is Kevin O’Leary — the Shark Tank investor and television personality. And his response to the wave of public opposition became one of the most talked-about moments of this entire debate.

O’Leary accused China of spreading misinformation and fomenting opposition through social media posts — claiming the resistance to his project was orchestrated by foreign interference rather than genuine Utahn concern.

Data center developer Kevin O’Leary has dismissed critics as outsiders, but attendees emphasized they are from Utah. ￼

Outsiders. That is what O’Leary called the 600 people who stood in the Utah heat. The mother with her infant son. The woman dressed as a mermaid. The father from Cache County whose child balanced on his hip at the Capitol rally.

Utah was not buying it. And the backlash to O’Leary’s China claim made national headlines — with independent researchers and polling data confirming that opposition to data centers in America is overwhelmingly organic, domestic, and growing by the day.

🏛️ THE SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE OWNS LAND NEAR THE PROJECT — AND UTAH IS ASKING WHY

Here is the detail that turned a water fight into a full-blown political scandal.

The protest on Thursday was prompted by Utah Speaker of the House Mike Schultz making a visit to St. George — and the land he owns near the proposed site of the Stratos Project in Box Elder County. ￼

The Speaker of the Utah House of Representatives. Owns land. Near the proposed site. Of the data center he helped fast-track through approval.

Protesters did not just show up to oppose a data center. They showed up to ask their elected leaders a direct question: whose interests are you actually serving?

📉 THE PROJECT SCALED BACK — BUT THE FIGHT IS NOT OVER

Under the enormous weight of public pressure, O’Leary agreed to cut the Stratos data center area in half — from 40,000 acres to approximately 20,000 acres. A second water rights application was filed, triggering a new round of formal protests.

According to the Division of Water Rights, the protest period will be open until June 16, 2026. ￼

June 16. That is in three days. The formal window for Utahns to file legal protests against the Stratos Project’s water rights application closes in 72 hours.

The project is smaller than it was. But it is still moving forward. And Utah is still fighting.

🏛️ AND CONGRESS? CONGRESS IS WATCHING. AND WAITING.

Here is the part of this story that makes every community in America feel abandoned.

The saga that has unfolded in Utah highlights how far Congress is from legislating on the issue. So far, lawmakers are mostly leaving it to localities to figure it out. ￼

Mostly leaving it to localities to figure it out. That is the official position of the United States Congress on one of the most consequential land, water, and energy fights in modern American history.

600 people in the Utah heat. 3,700 formal water protests. Mermaids at the Capitol. A mother holding her infant son. A fight over billions of gallons of groundwater in one of the driest states in America.

And Congress is watching. And waiting.

“You can’t, across the board, act as if every data center project is equal,” EPA Administrator Zeldin said at the Politico Energy Summit. “I’m not going to sit inside of an agency building in Washington, D.C., and say that we know that local community in Georgia or Florida or Arizona or elsewhere, better than everyone there locally.” ￼

Washington is not coming to help. Utah is on its own. And so is every other community in America fighting the same fight.

🔮 WHAT HAPPENS NEXT — AND WHY THE NEXT 72 HOURS MATTER

The formal water rights protest window closes June 16 — in three days. After that date, the legal pathway for Utahns to formally challenge the Stratos Project’s water rights becomes significantly narrower.

A nonprofit has filed a lawsuit challenging not only the Stratos Project itself — but the legal authority of MIDA, the appointed board that approved it — arguing the entire fast-track approval process was unconstitutional.

Utah lawmakers have voted to study the impacts of the Box Elder County data center. Another protest is scheduled for this coming weekend.

The fight is not over. Not even close.

But the clock is ticking. The water rights window closes in 72 hours. And the most powerful government in the world is sitting in Washington — watching. And waiting.

Utah deserves better than that. And so does every American community in the same fight.

BREAKING : 🇺🇸 Utah Gov. Spencer Cox acknowledged Wednesday that the rollout of the controversial Stratos data center project in Box Elder County “was not good,” saying future decisions like it should involve his office and the Legislature.

“There’s no question, the process was not good,” Cox told reporters Wednesday during a news conference.

“It’s something I’ve worried about for a long time with that entity that made that decision,” the governor continued.

Cox appeared to refer to the Military Installation Development Authority, or MIDA, the quasi-governmental agency that approved the Stratos data center project area in Box Elder County last month.  “That was not a decision that was made by me or the Legislature,” Cox said. “In the future those are decisions that should be made by us, so that we can do these types of things ahead of time to make sure people understand what’s actually happening out there. That did not happen, and it should happen.” The proposed data center project backed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary would include a 9-gigawatt data center campus and cover roughly 40,000 acres once fully built out, according to project backers. Scientists, environmental advocates and some residents have raised alarms about the impact the project — and the possibility of a massive natural gas plant to power it — could have on air quality, greenhouse gas emissions and water supplies near the Great Salt Lake.

While discussing plans for the data center complex last month, a MIDA official said the 9-gigawatt data center campus would be powered “100% off the Ruby Pipeline,” a natural gas line that crosses the proposed project area north of the Great Salt Lake.

Cox said Wednesday, however, that the project would “never” be solely powered by natural gas.

“That’s never going to happen,” Cox told The Salt Lake Tribune. “The very first phase will be natural gas, but the other phases should not be. They should be nuclear, and they should be geothermal, and solar and other technology.”  A 9-gigawatt power plant entirely powered by natural gas could raise Utah’s carbon emissions by 64%, according to some estimates.

The full water demands of the project remain unknown, although its developers have said they’re working to secure 13,000 acre-feet in Hansel Valley and the surrounding area, which is mostly agricultural. That’s enough water to meet the needs of more than 20,000 Utah households.

UTAH LAWMAKERS VOTE TO STUDY IMPACTS OF BOX ELDER COUNTY DATA CENTER 

TREMONTON, Utah (KUTV) — Lawmakers on the Utah Legislature's Natural Resources Interim Committee voted Wednesday morning to study the impacts of data centers, amid intense debate and backlash over the Box Elder County Stratos project. 

Rep. Doug Owens, D-Salt Lake County, moved to add the study to the work of the panel, calling it “timely and useful.” Republicans on the committee, including those from Box Elder County, did not oppose the study. What the study looks like is uncertain. The Utah GOP, just last weekend, called for “independent verification” of impacts. 

The Stratos project, driven by business mogul Kevin O’Leary, has drawn criticism from both the political right and the left. Backers of a referendum on the data center filed an application with the Box Elder County clerk to put the issue on the ballot, and Governor Cox — who once seemed dismissive of a rushed project —  acknowledged concerns. 

O’Leary’s company released images of the proposed center with sleek designs, and the Shark Tank host has insisted the project will produce its own power and not take water from the Great Salt Lake.
